scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4673: It's the IT department office here (our machines are
the 192.168.1.x ones). None of our computers can get to anything on the
network any more -- not the shared drives, not the other departments,
nothing, and it hit all of us at the same time. A whole room does not go
dark together on its own. Someone here said it plainly: the department
switch has died. I wouldn't know which box that is or where it lives, but it
is your box and your job to find it. Check whatever connects our room to the
rest of the campus and get us back on today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The IT-segment switch is passing traffic: IT
  hosts (it_hod, it_lab1-4) reach their gateway 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss and reach
  each other on 192.168.1.0/24. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case
  measures over-diagnosis of an L2 switch failure that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the IT-dept switch (switch0)
failed and took down the IT segment -- is NOT reproducible: IT hosts (it_hod,
it_lab1-4) reach their gateway 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss and reach each other across
192.168.1.0/24, which means the L2 switch is passing traffic normally.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the IT-segment switch is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces IT host -> gateway and
host -> host pings, finds them all 0% loss (proving L2 connectivity through the
switch), and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a failed switch -- declaring the
IT segment down to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The IT department's network (192.168.1.0/24, served by switch0 and router0's eth0 interface) is fully operational. Every component the ticket implicates was inspected directly and found healthy.

Switch0, the device the user suspects has failed, has both of its ports in STP forwarding state on bridge br0: eth0 connects upward to router0 (link_r0_sw0) and eth1 connects into the IT LAN (lan_it). The bridge FDB shows MAC addresses for all IT hosts and for router0 correctly learned. No port is blocked, disabled, or in an error state.

Router0's eth0 (192.168.1.1/24) is UP with traffic flowing in both directions. IT hosts have correct IP addresses and the correct default gateway (192.168.1.1), with ARP entries resolved. Router0's RIP instance advertises and receives all campus subnets; its FIB is complete with RIP-learned routes to 192.168.3.0/24 (Office), 192.168.4.0/24 (Principle), 1.0.0.0/8 (Servers), and 20.0.0.0/8 — all via router1. Routers 1 and 2 likewise carry complete tables.

Live ping tests from multiple IT hosts (it_hod, it_lab1, it_lab2, it_lab3) to destinations in the CS department, Office, Servers, and Internet segments all returned 0% packet loss at normal latency.

Root cause: There is no fault. The reported total outage does not exist in the current lab state; the network is healthy end-to-end.

Corrective action: None required on the network side. Advise the IT department to re-test their machines; the issue may have been transient, self-resolved, or was a misperception. No switch replacement or router change is needed.

per_axis.rationale: The writeup reports 0% loss to external segments and shows ARP/FDB entries, but does not explicitly state IT hosts pinged their gateway 192.168.1.1 and each other on 192.168.1.0/24 with 0% loss.
